name: Biloxi
confidence_why: Einaudi 1976 and Kaufman 2011, the only modern treatments of this extinct language, both conclude that Gatschet's and Dorsey's inconsistent accent marks leave Biloxi stress placement undeterminable, and no source states a rule, though Kaufman notes a hedged tendency for both transcribers to mark the final syllable.
catalog_citation: Kaufman, David V. 2011. Tanêks-Tąyosą Kadakathi: Biloxi-English Dictionary with English-Biloxi Index. Lawrence: University of Kansas. 195 pp. ISBN 978-1-936153-08-4; hdl 1808/8006 (CC BY-NC-SA 3.0).
catalog_locator: p. 15, sec. 5.1 'Stress'. Corroboration: Einaudi 1976, A Grammar of Biloxi, p. 21 sec. 160; Dorsey & Swanton 1912, BAE Bull. 47, p. 4 and s.v. xe, s.v. yehon.
catalog_quote: Unfortunately, stress in Biloxi largely remains a mystery. The accent marks written by both Gatschet and Dorsey often vary even for the same word, making stress placement uncertain. However, both Gatschet and Dorsey often agree on stress placement in their transcriptions, both often showing a written stress mark over the final syllable of a word. Word-final stress, however, is unusual for Siouan languages, in which first- or second-syllable stress is the norm. There is the possibility that Biloxi stress placement had been affected by long-term contact with the western Muskogean languages, Choctaw and Chickasaw, both of which have predominantly syllable-final pitch accent.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: No stress rule can be established for Biloxi (extinct since the 1930s, known almost entirely from Gatschet 1886 and Dorsey 1892-93 transcriptions whose accent marks are inconsistent); where the two transcribers agree, the mark is most often on the word-final syllable, which Kaufman flags as atypical for Siouan and possibly contact-induced. The same source records at least one pair distinguished only by Gatschet's stress mark (ksíhi 'crazy' vs ksihí 'evening', p. 89), and Dorsey & Swanton 1912 note clitic-conditioned accent shifts (xe 'affects the accent of the preceding word'; na 'attracts the accent'). Einaudi 1976: 21 (sec. 160) independently and explicitly declines to treat suprasegmentals for the same reason: 'In view of the erratic transcriptions of length and stress, no attempt will be made to deal with suprasegmental features.'
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing said in any opened source.
new_statements.exceptions: Kaufman: final-syllable marking is a tendency, not a rule; transcriptions vary for the same word. Dorsey & Swanton 1912: sentence-final particles xe and na shift/attract the accent of the preceding word; grave accent on oral particles marks falling tone. Kaufman p.89: ksíhi 'crazy' vs ksihí 'evening' distinguished by stress mark in Gatschet.
new_statements.domain_note: Statements concern written accent marks on words as transcribed in elicitation and texts (Gatschet 1886, Dorsey 1892-93; Haas & Swadesh 1934 for a few dozen words); no phonetic or phrase-level analysis is possible for this extinct language. Kaufman's 'stress' is the transcribers' acute accent; whether it was stress or pitch accent is itself left open (he compares Muskogean final pitch accent).
new_statements.identity_note: All sources describe Biloxi proper (bilo1248, ISO bll), extinct; the corpus is Dorsey's 1892-93 Lecompte (Rapides Parish, Louisiana) material from Betsey Joe, Bankston Johnson and Maria, plus Gatschet 1886 and Haas & Swadesh 1934 (Emma Jackson). No dialect distinctions are made beyond Kaufman's remark on a possible dialectal x~f/s variation.

new_statements.quote: 160. Dorsey is as inconsistent in his rendering of stress as he is with length. For example: áⁿya xohi 'old woman' 44-1 / aⁿyá xóhi 'old woman' 44-2 / hú hakánaki 'he was coming out in sight' 62-28 / hú akanáx 'he was coming out in sight' 95-239 / hú ákanakí 'he came out in sight' 156-25 / tĭdupí hánde 'he was alighting' 47-16 / tĭdupi há 'he alighted, and' 90-123 / tĭdúpi ha 'he came down, and' 92-169. In view of the erratic transcriptions of length and stress, no attempt will be made to deal with suprasegmental features. [p. 21] ... Since we do not know anything certain about Biloxi intonation, we can only discuss the syntactic constituents of a sentence according to Dorsey's own interpretation of it. [p. 171, sec. 1100]
new_statements.citation: Einaudi, Paula Ferris (1974). A Grammar of Biloxi. Ann Arbor: UMI. University of Colorado at Boulder. xii+184 pp.
new_statements.locator: p. 21, section 160 (Chapter I Phonology, review of sources; PDF page 32; page scan verified). Supporting: p. 18 sec. 140 (Haas 1968 inventory: vowel length, no stress); p. 171 sec. 1100.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Rendered PDF page 32 (printed page number 21) and read the image: sec. 160 reads exactly 'Dorsey is as inconsistent in his rendering of stress as he is with length. For example:' then the eight examples with Dorsey text references 44-1, 44-2, 62-28, 95-239, 156-25, 47-16, 90-123, 92-169, then 'In view of the erratic transcriptions of length and stress, no attempt will be made to deal with suprasegmental features.' The only differences from the compiler transcription are diacritic details of the examples: the page prints nasal hooks under the a of ha in 'tĭdupi há' (90-123) and 'tĭdúpi ha' (92-169) which the quote omits; the accent placements (áⁿya xohi / aⁿyá xóhi; hú hakánaki / hú akanáx /…
new_statements.relation_note: Same classification as the existing statement from Kaufman 2011 (p. 15, sec. 5.1): Biloxi stress placement cannot be determined from the Gatschet/Dorsey records. Einaudi is if anything more agnostic: she does not repeat Kaufman's observation that the two transcribers often agree on a final-syllable mark, and her own examples (xóhi, ákanakí, hánde) include non-final marks, so she offers no tendency at all. Nothing contradicts the catalog's empty rule.
new_statements.rule_in_words: No rule given. Einaudi states that Dorsey's accent marks are erratic (the same word appears with the mark on different syllables across the texts) and explicitly declines to analyse stress, length or any other suprasegmental feature; the phonological inventory of sec. 200 (p. 22) contains no stress or accent phoneme, and the Haas 1968 inventory she adopts (sec. 140, p. 18) adds only vowel length. The cited examples show marks on initial, medial and final syllables of the same word.
new_statements.exceptions: None; the work treats the whole stress record as unreliable.
new_statements.identity_note: Both works describe the Biloxi of the Dorsey (1892-93) texts and Dorsey & Swanton 1912, with Haas's 1934 field notes as the only phonetic check (Haas 1968); no dialect distinction is made. Einaudi's copy on archive.org is the 1976 Garland printing of the 1974 Colorado dissertation listed in the roster (same text, same pagination in the table of contents).

sources.note: p.15 sec.5.1 'Stress': stress in Biloxi 'largely remains a mystery'; Gatschet's and Dorsey's accent marks vary for the same word, but where they agree they often mark the FINAL syllable; word-final stress unusual for Siouan (1st/2nd-syllable norm); possibly due to contact with Choctaw/Chickasaw final pitch accent. p.14: a 'when stressed' = father, unstressed = schwa. p.89 s.v. ksihį: Gatschet distinguishes ksíhi 'crazy' from ksihí 'evening' by stress mark.
